content.text: Students discuss the importance of characters from
Look Both Ways
changing their minds after considering other points of view.
Discussing how fictional characters from the anchor text share small, ordinary moments creates empathy, voice, and community.

Students will review their thinking and revise their writing during peer review. They will engage in more class discussion in Lesson 44. They will use similar speaking skills to present work to the large group in Lesson 45.
Public speaking is an Author’s Chair component of the Performance Task, along with reviewing and thinking as part of peer review and revision.
Look Both Ways
by Jason Reynolds
Unit 1 Lesson 36 Student Edition
Ordinary Moments Graphic Organizer (from Lesson 3)
Identify and share moments from
Look Both Ways
in which characters change their minds. Discuss the importance of these moments in building empathy, community, and civic responsibility.
Explain how perspective-sharing builds community by citing one moment from
Look Both Ways
, using reflective language (This helped me realize . . .), and using discussion protocol stems to build, clarify, and revise ideas in a Reflect & Respond Dialogue.
Students will identify and share moments from
Look Both Ways
in which characters change their minds. Students will also discuss the importance of these moments in building empathy, community, and civic responsibility.
Students will explain how perspective-sharing builds community by citing one moment from
Look Both Ways
, using reflective language (This helped me realize…), and using discussion protocol stems to build, clarify, and revise ideas in a Reflect & Respond Dialogue.
Reflect and Response Dialogue
Look through your
Ordinary Moments
graphic organizer and choose a moment when a character from
Look Both Ways
changed their mind. If you don’t have one yet, add one now. Next to that character’s name, write what made them change their mind and what effect it had on the plot and/or other characters.
Introduce New Words Using Morphemes
Target Word:
civic responsibility
Directions:
We’re learning about the phrase civic responsibility today. It is a concept that shows up throughout our reading, so let’s explore it more deeply.
Have you seen the phrase “civic responsibility”
before? Where?
“Responsibility” is taking care of or having control over something, but what does “civic” mean?
If “civic” means relating to being a citizen, then what is
civic responsibility

Throughout this unit, we’ve talked about how stories build empathy by helping readers understand other points of view. This builds community, because people who have empathy for others in their community also take their civic responsibility
seriously.
Part of being an empathetic citizen with civic responsibility is being willing to consider someone else’s point of view. Engaged citizens can even change their minds after listening to others.
As we discuss characters in
Look Both Ways
who changed their minds, we are going to listen to one another’s points of view and stay open to changing our own minds.
Some sentence frames you can use when discussing are: “I agree with you that _______, but I also think _______.” “Before, I thought _______, but after hearing your idea, now I think _______.”
Reflection
Reflection:
Self-reflect on the discussion strategies you just talked about, using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in your ability to have an academic discussion in which you listen to other points of view and are open to changing your mind?
Discussion on Changing Minds, Empathy, and Community:
Look Both Ways
Reflect and Response Dialogue
Directions:
Share with your partner the moment from the story that you chose. Explain why you think it’s important.
Partners, respond with the following sentence stem: “After hearing _____, I now think _____.”
Now we’re going to focus on the effects the characters’ change of mind had on them or on their community. Keep using sentence frames if you need them.
Checklist
Make sure you:
Come prepared with your ideas and evidence from the text.
Listen carefully and respond thoughtfully and respectfully to others.
Show understanding of different points of view by reflecting or paraphrasing what others say.
Use what you know about the characters to explain what they might say or do.
Reflection
Directions
: How can sharing stories help create a greater sense of civic responsibility?

Use this launch to connect students’ previous work on the Ordinary Moments graphic organizer to today’s discussion on empathy, community, and changing minds. Emphasize that reflecting on characters’ decisions helps us understand multiple perspectives and supports civic responsibility. As needed, model how to identify a moment when a character changes their mind and its impact on others, and show students how to cite evidence and use discussion stems. This sets the foundation for a structured, text-based academic discussion.
Have students take out the Ordinary Moments graphic organizers they began in Lesson 3 and have returned to throughout the unit.
Instruct students to review their graphic organizers and choose an example of a character who changed their mind.
Say:
Look through your organizer and choose a moment when a character from
Look Both Ways
changed their mind. If you don’t have one yet, add one now. Next to that character’s name, write what made them change their mind and what effect it had on the plot and/or other characters.

Stevie changes his mind about helping Marcus and his friends take Pia’s skateboard. It’s too late, and he can’t find her to apologize the next day. This leads him to ask many questions about his own conflicts at school.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, we’re going to discuss examples from
Look Both Ways
of characters changing their minds and the effects these changes have on their communities.
Students will use their Ordinary Moments graphic organizer to choose a moment from the anchor text to discuss in which a character changes their mind about something.
Introduce New Words Using Morphemes
Target Word:
civic responsibility
Say these Directions:
We’re learning about the phrase
civic responsibility
today. It is a concept that shows up throughout our reading, so let’s explore it more deeply.
Introduce the Word:
Write or project “civic responsibility” where all students can see it. Ask a volunteer to say it out loud.
Ask:
Have you seen the phrase “
civic responsibility
before? Where?
Identify the Component Words
: Students are likely to be familiar with the word “responsibility,” but less so with “civic.”
Ask:
“Responsibility” is taking care of or having control over something, but what does “civic” mean?
Identify the Root:
Underline the root -civ in “civic.” Explain that -civ comes from Latin civis, meaning “citizen.”
Language Connection:
Write or project the words “civic,” “civil,” and “civilization,” and underline the -civ root in each. Explain that all these words relate to people living together as citizens in a society.
Identify Affixes:
Circle -ic in “civic.”
Say:
The suffix -
ic
means “of or relating to.” Someone who is artistic is connected to art. Something that is
metallic
is
made of metal
Language Connection:
The Spanish word for civic is “civica,” and Spanish also uses the Latin root
-civ
in many other words, such as “civilización.”
Determine Meaning:
Ask:
If “civic” means relating to being a citizen, then what is
civic responsibility
? [the duty that you have as a citizen to participate in your democracy]
Discuss Connections to Today’s Discussion and Model Discussion Strategies:
Recall earlier discussions of how stories build empathy and community. Relate this idea to civic responsibility.
Say:

Throughout this unit, we’ve talked about how stories build empathy by helping readers understand other points of view. This builds community because people who have empathy for others in their community also take their
civic responsibility
seriously.
Transition to today’s discussion and model discussion strategies.
Say:
Part of being an empathetic citizen with
civic responsibility
is being willing to consider someone else’s point of view. Engaged citizens can even change their minds after listening to others.
Say:
As we discuss characters in
Look Both Ways
who changed their minds, we are going to listen to one another’s points of view and stay open to changing our own minds.
Say:
Some sentence frames you can use when discussing are: “I agree with you that _______, but I also think _______.” “Before, I thought _______, but after hearing your idea, now I think _______.”
Say:

For example, I might say, “I agree with you that Stevie changing his mind about taking Pia’s skateboard was important, because it showed that he wanted to do better.” My partner might say, “I agree with you that it’s important, but I also think he changes his mind too late.” I could reply, “I agree with you that Stevie changes his mind too late, but I also think that changing his mind and telling his mom will probably change him in ways that will affect the community.” My partner may then say, “Before, I thought Stevie changing his mind didn’t matter because it already happened, but after hearing your idea, I think maybe it has effects that we just don’t see yet.”

By the end of this launch, students should be prepared to identify a character’s moment when they change their mind and explain its effect on the plot or other characters. They should understand that recognizing these moments is the first step toward analyzing empathy, community, and civic responsibility in discussion. Students will be ready to participate meaningfully in the Reflect and Response Dialogue.
Help students to unpack civic responsibility through morphology and to use reflective discussion language to connect “changing minds” to empathy and community.
Display “civic responsibility.” Explicitly teach both parts: civic + responsibility.
Underline -civ- in “civic” and connect to “civil,” “civilization” to anchor meaning.
Circle -ic and remind students it means “related to.”
Require students to write one sentence applying the term to today’s discussion: Civic responsibility means… so in our discussion I will…
Model 1 “change-my-mind” exchange using the sentence frames. Then have students rehearse with a partner.
“Civic means ___, so civic responsibility is ___.”
“At first, I thought ___. Now I realize ___ because ___.”
“I agree with you that ___, and I want to add ___.”
“After hearing ___, I now think ___.”
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become more independent.
Emerging:
"At first, ___. Later, ___." / "This shows the character changed because ___."
Expanding:
"At first, ___. Later, ___. This shows ___." / "This moment helps us understand ___."
Bridging:
"By the end of the vignette, ___ comes to ___." / "This shift reflects the unit theme of ___ because ___."
Affirm that changing your mind is a strength in a community: it shows listening, humility, and care for others.
Revoice definitions into action: “Civic responsibility is…” → “So, during discussion, civic responsibility looks like…”
Upgrade vague talk: “It matters” → “This matters because it affects ___ in the community.”
Press for evidence: “Which moment shows the mind change?” → “Point to the scene/quote and name what changed.”
If students define civic responsibility too broadly → Prompt: “Add citizen/community language: ‘as a member of our community…’”
If students discuss feelings without a text moment → Prompt: “Name the character + the moment + what changed.”
If students struggle to revise thinking → Prompt: “Use the frame: ‘Before…, but after…, now…’”
Student can define civic responsibility using the morphology of -civ- and -ic.
Student uses at least 1 reflective stem (At first…, Now I realize…).
Student references a specific character and moment (not just a general event).

Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to support and expand student use of academic language, and provide scaffolding as needed.
Emerging:
Names one mind-changing moment using a frame; points to evidence.
Expanding:
Explains how a mind-change builds empathy; cites moments with brief reasoning.
Bridging:
Analyzes how mind-changes build empathy / community / civic responsibility; cites specific moments and connects to theme.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, we’re going to discuss examples of characters changing their minds in
Look Both Ways
and the effects it had on them and their communities. As we discuss, we’ll practice listening to one another’s points of view and staying open to changing our minds, which is part of our
civic responsibility
as classmates.
Reflection
Self-reflect on the discussion strategies you just talked about, using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to have an academic discussion in which you listen to other points of view and are open to changing your mind?
Students will use morphology to determine the meaning of the target phrase “civic responsibility” and discuss how this idea applies to changing one’s mind and being open to different points of view.
Discussion on Changing Minds, Empathy, and Community: Text: Look Both Ways (SL.6.1a, RL.6.3) (30 minutes)

Use this section to guide students through the Reflect and Response Dialogue routine. Begin by modeling one discussion exchange, emphasizing how to identify a character’s change in thinking, cite evidence, and explain its effects on the community. The goal is for students to connect character analysis to empathy and civic responsibility while practicing evidence-based speaking.
Reflect and Response Dialogue
Remind students briefly of how a
Reflect and Response Dialogue
routine works.
Say:

In a Reflect and Response Dialogue, you will choose a quote or part of the story you think is important. Then you will explain to a partner why you think it is important. Your partner will share their thoughts, and you’ll switch places. You will repeat this routine with a few different partners.
Say:
In today’s Reflect and Response Dialogue, we’re looking for a part of the story where a character changes their mind about something.
Practice one round with the class, cuing response stems as needed.
Say these Directions:
Share with your partner the moment from the story that you chose. Explain why you think it’s important.
Say:
Partners, respond with the following sentence stem: “After hearing _____, I now think _____.”

[Student A]: I chose the moment when the old men in the pool hall change their minds and decide to buy the Low Cuts’ candy. I think it’s important because it shows how the Low Cuts knew how important nostalgia would be to those guys. [Student B]: After hearing [Student A] explain the moment when the old men change their minds, now I think this wasn’t just important because it showed how smart the Low Cuts are, but also because it showed what was important to these other characters.
Teacher Tip
Students often retell what happened without naming the actual change in thinking. They describe the event but not the before/after shift. If you hear this, prompt: "What did the character think
before
? What do they think
now
? Say it in one sentence."

After a few minutes, instruct students to rotate to different partners and complete another round of discussion. At this point, stop providing cues for responses. Allow students to discuss independently.
Note to Teacher:

Round 1 establishes a shared foundation: every student has named a specific character moment. Round 2 pushes students from identification to analysis: what effect did this change have on the community? This sequencing mirrors the move from RL.6.3 (how characters respond/change) to the deeper thinking about empathy and civic responsibility.
With around ten minutes remaining, introduce the next prompt.
Say:
Now we’re going to focus on the effects the characters’ change of mind had on them or on their community. Keep using sentence frames if you need them.

[Student A]: I think the old men changing their minds about buying the Low Cuts’ candy affected the community because it made them think differently about the kids who live there. They saw that the kids were clever, and the kids saw that the old men had a soft spot. This might mean they’re all more willing to help each other later, which shows their civic responsibility. [Student B]: Before, I thought that this was only important because it shows the old men changing their minds, but now I also see that it’s important because the kids saw a different side too.

By the end of this discussion, students should be able to explain how a character’s change in thinking affects themselves and their community, citing textual evidence and using reflective language. They should demonstrate active listening, respectful responses, and the ability to revise their thinking in response to peers’ perspectives.
Support students to discuss mind-change moments using the Reflect and Response Dialogue so they practice evidence-based speaking, reflective revision, and community-building language.
Validate multiple interpretations as long as students anchor them in the text and speak respectfully.
Require each student to enter the routine with: character + moment + what changed + why (from the Ordinary Moments GO).
Round 1 prompt (Moment): “Name the moment and what changed.”
Round 2 prompt (Effect): “Explain the effect on the character and/or community.”
Post and point to the response stems during Round 1; remove prompts gradually by Round 2.
Midway stop: ask students to add one evidence phrase: “In the text, ___ shows ___.”
“The character changes their mind when ___; before they thought ___, but then ___.”
“This helped build empathy because ___.”
“This builds community because people ___ after hearing/learning ___.”
“I agree with you that ___, but I also think ___.”
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“In ___, ___ changed when ___.” / “One reason was ___.”
Expanding:
“In ___, ___ changed when ___, which suggests ___ about civic responsibility.”
Bridging:
“In ___, ___ changed when ___, which suggests ___ about civic responsibility; building on ___’s idea, this connects to community because ___.”
Revoice summaries into interpretation: “He apologized” → “That suggests he realized ___.”
Press for community link: “How does this change affect others?” → “This builds community because ___.”
Strengthen evidence referencing: “when they…” → “in the scene where ___ / the line that says ___.”
If students retell without stating the change → Prompt: “Say the ‘before/after’ in one sentence.”
If students can’t connect to community → Prompt: “Who else is affected? What might change in how they treat one another?”
If students disagree harshly → Prompt: “Start with one agreement and then offer: ‘Another way to see it is…’”
Student states a clear before/after change in thinking.
Student uses 1 evidence reference (scene/quote detail).
Student uses 1 reflective move showing revision (After hearing…, now I think…).
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Names a character + moment + what changed using a frame.
Expanding:
Includes character + moment + what changed + why; uses interpretive verbs (suggests/realized).
Bridging:
Connects mind-change moments to civic responsibility and community-building; revises summaries into interpretations with precise evidence.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Adding to a response
Remind students of sentence frames for adding to a response. Ex. I agree with you that ________, but I would also like to add ________.
Struggling with: Disagreeing with a response

Remind students of sentence frames for respectfully disagreeing with a response. Encourage them to find something in the response that they do agree with. Ex. I agree with you that ________, but I think another way to look at it is ________.
Struggling with: Changing their minds after hearing a response
Remind students of sentence frames for changing their minds. Ex. Before, I thought ________, but after hearing ________, I think ________.
Ready for extension: Evaluating the impact of a character changing their mind
Ask:
What do you think this character does differently after they change their mind? I think Stevie apologizes to Pia and eventually makes friends with her, while avoiding Marcus the best he can.
Checklist
Make sure you:
Come prepared with your ideas and evidence from the text.
Listen carefully and respond thoughtfully and respectfully to others.
Show understanding of different points of view by reflecting or paraphrasing what others say.
Use what you know about the characters to explain what they might say or do.
Learning in Action: Discussion on Changing Minds, Empathy, and Community: Text:
Look Both Ways
Students will use a Reflect and Response dialogue to discuss characters in
Look Both Ways
who change their minds, considering the impact of such changes on the characters and their communities.
Reflection

Use this reflection to consolidate students’ thinking about how sharing stories builds understanding, empathy, and civic responsibility. Encourage them to write brief, text-supported reflections using the optional sentence starter. Highlight how today’s discussion strategies can be applied beyond the classroom, reinforcing the connection between understanding others’ perspectives and participating responsibly in a community.
Invite students to reflect on today’s discussion by writing a brief response to the following prompt:
Say these Directions:
How can sharing stories help create a greater sense of
civic responsibility
Optional
Sentence Starter:
“Sharing stories helps us ____.”

Sharing stories helps us understand one another’s points of view, which builds empathy. When people in a community have more empathy, they also have a sense of civic responsibility to help and take care of one another.
Students will reflect on today’s discussion by writing about how sharing stories can create a sense of civic responsibility.
Instruct students to complete any narrative tasks that may remain unfinished and continue to brainstorm in their
Journal
about what they will write about in the Showcase Task:
Continue to generate ideas for the Showcase Task under the prompt:
Write a personal narrative based on an ordinary moment from your life.

standards.description: Describe how a particular story’s or drama’s plot unfolds in a series of episodes as well as how the characters respond or change as the plot moves toward a resolution.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering detailed questions, with minimal prompting and support.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering basic questions, with prompting and substantial support.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering detailed questions, with occasional prompting and moderate support.
